en: The Commentary on the Essential Meaning of the Noble Mother Prajñāpāramitā in Nine Verses,
Volume One,
composed by the Bodhisattva Śrīmatī Raktāmbara.
The wisdom of the Prajñāpāramitā is a mass of accumulated virtues and a treasury of merit;
all the various pāramitās are its primordial nature, eternally abiding.
Free from all conceptual proliferation and without obstruction, it is free from all discrimination and attains peace.
Supremely subtle and without intrinsic nature, transcending all names, signs, and characteristics,
he employs skillful means to proclaim the Dharma of the three vehicles; yet the characteristics attained through those three vehicles are all causes for the wisdom of omniscience.
I prostrate to the Prajñāpāramitā, the supreme wisdom that reaches the further shore.
Those who desire to practice correct contemplation should, in accordance with reason, reflect upon and discern the meaning of these nine verses in their entirety and in brief.
The nine verses state:
Arising through the predominance of karma, That which is known as the characteristic of the six sense bases—
This very thing is said to arise again, Its cause appearing like a shadow.
Like a city conjured by illusion, the observer is likewise a conjuration;
just as those forms are seen, so too is the world conjured by karma.
All sounds of the Dharma being taught are themselves the realm of hearing.
All things are like echoes, Conditioned by causes, they constitute the heard and the hearer.
The smelling of fragrances and the perceiving of tastes, As well as attachment to the objects of touch and so forth— All these are like dreams; Though attained, they are non-existent.
Just as a person is formed by a magical wheel, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are without reality;
just as that person is formed by the wheel, the body-wheel likewise has no self.
Whatever is variously obtained arises in the extreme brevity of a single moment.
This is like a mirage; upon being seen, it perishes and is without marks.
That which is grasped is like a reflection, arising from the mind since beginningless time;
thus, those marks and consciousness are mutually like reflections.
When one observes within one's own pure seeds, if the moon of wisdom appears,
it is like the moon reflected in water— manifest yet non-existent.
If that wisdom is in accord [with reality], it is the very nature of space.
Therefore, that which is known by wisdom is entirely like the nature of space.
As the preceding verse says:
"For those who desire to correctly contemplate all supreme wisdom that has reached the other shore,"
"One should contemplate the meaning of those nine verses in brief and according to reason.
What is called "superior wisdom" refers to the characteristics of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
"Pāra" (the other shore) means "limit.
"To go" means to arrive; that is, to arrive at the ultimate limit, reaching the state free from all conceptual discrimination. Thus it continues until this meaning is fully concluded.
"Correct observation" (*samyag-darśana*) refers to the non-erroneous characteristic.
"Zealous desire" (*chanda*) has the nature of mental attention (*manasikāra*) characterized by aspiration.
"That meaning" (*tad-artha*) refers to the meaning present at the time those nine verses were spoken; "meaning" (*artha*) here signifies the gateway to the meaning (*arthamukha*).
"Discernment" (vicāra) refers to contemplation and decisive selection.
What is it that is contemplated?
The verse provides a summary.
"Summary" (*saṃkṣepa*) means that which encompasses the whole and condenses the details.
Here, one should ask:
for what reason is it explained in summary?
Answer:
It is for the sake of enabling those of dull faculties to understand its meaning.
Having previously set forth nine verses, they are now explained in their proper sequence.
The first verse says:
"Arising through the predominance of karma, that which is called the characteristic of the six sense bases—
this very thing is said to arise again, its cause appearing like a shadow."
"Karma" refers to wholesome and unwholesome karma.
"Predominant" means that karma is predominant;
by the predominant power of those various karmas, birth itself arises.
From what is it produced?
The verse says: "The characteristic of the six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
A "base" (*āyatana*) refers to that which serves as the support for consciousness and the locus from which it arises; therefore, it is called a "base."
What, then, is this? It refers to the six internal bases, such as the eye and so forth.
The term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) used in the verse has the meaning of "that which marks or indicates."
If these six sense bases arise from causes, then those very same factors likewise give rise to further phenomena.
This statement thus establishes the ultimate and definitive conclusion of this meaning.
Question:
What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)?
The verse explains this itself by stating, "The cause is like a reflected image," using the appearance of a reflection as a metaphor.
Within these reflected appearances, all agents, actions, and the objects of action are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature and are empty.
This point is now concluded.
Furthermore, regarding the production from the intrinsic natures of the six external bases, such as form and so forth, I shall now demonstrate them one by one in succession.
The second verse says:
"Like a city conjured by illusion, the observer is also a conjuration;
just as those perceived forms appear, so too is the world conjured by karma."
It is just like a city conjured by illusory phenomena; the observer who later perceives it is likewise a conjuration.
Both of them do not exist. Why is this?
Because their nature arises from what is unreal, both the seer and the seen—those two forms characterized by external resistance—are all transformations of karma.
What is perceived within the three realms of the world is like that; thus, the principle is the same.
This transformation is non-different in nature from that which is transformed; therefore, the following verse says: "Like a sound facing its echo.
To establish this meaning, the third verse states:
"All sounds of those who preach the Dharma Are themselves the objects of hearing."
"All things are like echoes; hearing and the object heard are established through conditions.
What is called "the teaching of the Dharma" arises from the predominance of the speaker; the sound directed toward that [speaker] is the objective sphere of hearing.
If one hears that the objective sphere is thus, all other phenomena likewise arise in this manner; therefore, the analogy of sound meeting its echo is employed.
Since this sound and its echo are the same as other phenomena, the term "all" is used here without distinction.
What is called "conditioned arising" (pratyaya-siddha) means that hearing is so called because it is established through conditions such as hearing itself.

If all that exists is of a nature produced by action, then both the hearer and the heard are entirely established through conditions within the sphere of apprehension; therefore, all sounds are like echoes.
The meaning thus explained is ultimate; therefore, the following verse says: "All is like a dream.
To establish this point, the fourth verse states:
"Smelling fragrances and perceiving tastes, Attachment to objects such as touch..."
"All this is like a dream; though attained, it is non-existent.
As for the phrase "smelling odors," it refers to the objective sphere of olfactory consciousness—the various odors that constitute the nature of all created things which are smelled.
"Discerning tastes" refers to the objective sphere of the tongue-consciousness, which discerns various tastes and so forth.
"Tangibility" refers to the objective sphere of the body-consciousness, which perceives various tangibles and so forth.

Within such various objects of experience, one seeks and delights in them, giving rise to attachment; thus, one becomes bound to each respective object, experiencing the distinct sensations of fragrance, flavor, touch, and so forth, according to those specific attachments.
If one gives rise to the mark of apprehension regarding those objects, they are found to be unobtainable; therefore, the verse says, "All are like dreams.
"All" here signifies the sense of non-differentiation.
Nevertheless, the internal bases such as the eye and the external bases such as form do indeed exist.
If this were not so, how could the activity of an agent be initiated?
To dispel this doubt, the fifth verse states:
"Just as a phantom wheel creates a person, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are devoid of reality;
just as that [phantom] performs various actions, so too the wheel of the body is without self.
For example, by means of the method of the phantom wheel, the marks of a human body are produced; that person created by the phantom possesses all manner of activities.
It is also like a person who, though nominally possessing an agent and an action performed, further possesses the characteristics of movement such as coming and going.
The word "all" (*sarva*) in the verse signifies the meaning of various classifications of what is produced.
What is it that acts?
It is the body produced by illusion.
Since such a body is formed through illusory phenomena, that very illusory body is in reality devoid of self.
"Non-" (*a-*) signifies the sense of being devoid of; "self" (*ātman*) refers to a sovereign master.
This expression "non-self" (*anātman*) means being devoid of a self.

Therefore, there is no agent herein, for in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), nothing whatsoever exists. Thus, the verse says: "The activity of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is without reality."
"Non-substantiality" (asāra) means the sense of lacking power or capacity.
Now, in this case, there is such a lack of power and capacity because this agent lacks a sovereign master.
If a person created by illusion has no sovereign controller, it appears despite having no reality;
so too are all phenomena ultimately without reality. One should understand here that there is no distinction in this sense; thus, the subsequent verse says, "like a mirage."
To establish this meaning, the sixth verse states:
"If various things are obtained, they arise in extreme moments;
these are like a mirage—upon seeing them, they perish and lack defining characteristics."
"Various" means of many kinds.
"That which is obtained" refers to the characteristics of the objects of apprehension as they are conceptually constructed through differentiation.
Those apprehended objects arise for an extremely brief moment; this moment-to-moment occurrence is called an "extreme moment."
"Arising" (*jāti*) has the meaning of "origination," which refers to that which originates within an ultimate moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Since there is origination within an ultimate moment, all those various phenomena that originate from an ultimate moment are impermanent; this is the final conclusion of the matter.

The Essential Meaning of the Noble Mother Prajñāpāramitā in Nine Verses,
Volume Two.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Śrīguṇapāla;

translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Dispersing Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Dharmapāla, and others, by imperial decree. Herein it should be asked:
What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) within that ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)?
Answer:
The verse uses the metaphor of "being like a mirage.

A "mirage" refers to the false conjunction of three factors—dust from the earth, sunlight, and space—which, like a gathering of mirages, is perceived at first and then vanishes. Therefore, the verse says: "Upon seeing it, it perishes; it is without marks."
The same principle applies to all various objects of perception that are individually apprehended: although each is distinctly manifested, they all lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Why is this?
Because their respective natures are not consistent across preceding and succeeding moments, and because their natures are not identical.
The foolish grasp at them and revolve within the notion of a single nature; therefore, all such [beings] fall into the realms of mundane existence.

Furthermore, herein, if both the grasper and the grasped are empty of obstructive nature, then their intrinsic nature is luminous and primordially unarisen, and the manifestation of mental phenomena is like a reflection.
To explain this meaning, the seventh verse says:
"The grasped object is like a reflection; Arising from the mind since beginningless time, Both its characteristics and consciousness Are mutually like reflections."
Regarding the statement that "the apprehended object is like a reflection," this means that it resembles that [original object].
What is it that it resembles?
It is like the images of faces and so forth seen within mirrors and the like.
What does this mean?

It means that [the object] arises from the mind, because it is produced solely by the mind; thus, the mind itself is bound to the existence of its apprehended external objects and so forth, having the nature of not relinquishing them.
This meaning is concluded.

Furthermore, just as the image of a face in an external mirror that is grasped, so too do those various phenomena, through the seeds of habitual practice, cause the mind to apprehend them; thus, within non-duality, one perceives the characteristics of duality and mutual obstruction.

Since beginningless time, those things produced from the mind—such as reflected images—are examined as objects, whether simultaneously or sequentially; they all lack intrinsic nature and are not merely mental phenomena. Nevertheless, by means of the characteristics of the object, they are able to induce the perceiving consciousness; therefore, they possess characteristics.
Generally speaking, the term "characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) has the meaning of being subsumed and collected.
It is not that only the object of apprehension possesses such characteristics; the subject of apprehension is likewise so.
The intended meaning here is that the object of apprehension lacks intrinsic nature and the subject of apprehension is unreal.
The verse says "mutually.
"Mutually" means "in combination"; they are mutually combined, all like reflections.

Because they are like reflections, the nature of the non-separation between those two—the grasper and the grasped—is such that, within the state of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), those two phenomena manifest as objects of apprehension from that mental factor.

The general meaning of this is as follows: the intrinsic nature of that mind is primordially luminous, devoid of the dualistic characteristics of subject and object; it is fundamentally free from the defilements of ignorance such as attachment, and is pure, pristine, and detached from all grasping.
Therefore, the following verse says, "like the moon in water.
To explain this meaning, the eighth verse states:
"If the moon of wisdom appears Within one's own pure seeds,"
"It is like the moon in water; though appearing before one, it has no real existence.
"Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) is defined as meditative concentration (*samādhi*); concentration refers to the characteristic of one-pointedness of mind.
Within that meditative concentration, there is an object of contemplation because the mind possesses mastery.
The verse uses the term "self" (*sva*), which means that the purification of one's own seeds is itself purity.
"Purity" (*viśuddhi*) means being free from turbidity.
It is produced from the seeds of one's own body, speech, and mind, arising as a conceptualization through the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

The syllable *Hrīḥ* transforms into a pervasive, blazing radiance; from within that light, nectar-light issues forth from the seed of the heart, shining extensively. That light further becomes an immense wheel of fire, and from upon that wheel of fire, wisdom and skillful means emerge.
Furthermore, from this, the syllable-gateway *Ha* arises.

That syllable vibrates with a great sound, and within it appears an eight-petaled lotus flower; the syllable *Ha* resides in its center, and one should visualize sixteen positions distributed both internally and externally.
Again, visualize the syllable *ka* (*kā*) forming, surrounded on all sides by the host of constellations.
Furthermore, in the corresponding directions, visualize the Buddha-lotuses; each of their sixteen parts becomes a lunar disc.

Having observed in this way, one further visualizes the syllable HŪṂ appearing within the pure seed-syllable upon it, endowed with blazing light; from within that light, a great fire with intense, blazing flames emerges.
One should contemplate that from the moon of wisdom within oneself, the bodhicitta arises; from this, in turn, the vajra-wisdom moon arises.
One should know that this moon is the vajra-wisdom pervading the world, its light of wisdom illuminating all forms and appearances.
Therefore, the verse says: "When the moon of wisdom appears.

That Wisdom-Vajra accomplishment gives birth to the signs of the peerless nirvāṇa consisting of prajñā and upāya; furthermore, from that prajñā arises the form of the Bodhisattva Māmakī within the Vajradhātu. One should visualize this profound, supreme, and most secret samāpatti, with dense clouds of secrecy spreading everywhere to manifest universal radiance.
That Bodhisattva has a blue-colored body with eight arms and three faces:
the front face is blue, the right face is yellow, and the left face is white;
the first right hand holds a sword, the second holds an arrow, the third holds a hook, and the fourth holds a vajra.
The first left hand holds a wheel, the second holds a bow, the third holds a lasso, and the fourth holds a bell.
Thus, that Bodhisattva’s wisdom and skillful means are in perfect union, such that all his actions accord with expedient means.
Adorned with all the various marks, he wears a crown of Akṣobhya Buddha upon his head and manifests a joyful and lovely countenance, sitting in the full lotus posture.

Like the *ātasi* flower of pure clarity possessing the most excellent circular halo of the sun, and like the nature of Great Bliss, the Vajrasattva, he sprinkles nectar everywhere throughout all things.
The body of this bodhisattva is itself the body of the Tathāgata, produced from wisdom and skillful means.
Therefore, the verse says, "like the moon in water.
The word "if" (若) in the verse carries the meaning of "as" (如), because it is like the moon in water.

This is itself emptiness; from within these empty phenomena all phenomena arise, yet that which arises is by nature originally unarisen. Therefore, it is metaphorically described as being like the moon reflected in water.
In this regard, if one grasps at the existence of intrinsic nature within the self-nature of the dharmadhātu, there is in fact no such nature. Why?
Because the verse states: "There is nothing present."

Because, within suchness where all phenomena are non-apprehendable, there is nothing that can be performed or realized; indeed, were there anything performed or realized, it would all be the conventional establishment of phenomena, equal to space.
To establish this meaning, the ninth verse states:
“If the wisdom of one who is in union Is itself the characteristic of space,
then that which is known by such wisdom is entirely like the characteristic of space.”
Regarding the term "conjunction" (yoga), it should be understood as the conjunction of the two dharmas of wisdom and meditative concentration.
That conjunction is itself the vajra; because one possesses that dharma of conjunction, one is called a "conjoined one" (yogin).

The wisdom possessed by those who are thus associated gives rise to the body of the Tathāgata through the skillful means of insight within the state where all phenomena are without grasping and free from dualistic characteristics; it is not, as previously described, the nature of conceptual proliferation such as the aggregates, bases, and elements.
This meaning is now concluded.
However, the body of the Tathāgata is formed from the self-nature of the unmoving dharma-realm and is fundamentally unarisen. Why is this so?
Because the Tathāgata and others are by nature free from self-nature, they are thus without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and are ultimately inexpressible.
"Without intrinsic nature" means that they are originally unarisen; therefore, they are called "without intrinsic nature."
Therefore, the verse says, "like the nature of space.
What does this mean?

It means that because it is free from the nature of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is like space; and since space has such a characteristic, one should investigate the correspondence with space in accordance with reality in this manner.
"Characteristic" (lakṣaṇa) means that which marks or indicates.

Furthermore, it should be understood that regarding the unobstructed intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all phenomena, that which performs a function refers to the characteristics of the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) by which wisdom enters the three realms.

The phrase "having the characteristic of space" indicates that the nature of the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)—consisting of the aggregates, bases, and elements, as well as the two worlds of sentient beings and the environment—is manifested in accordance with the objects of knowledge through ignorance; thus, these objects of knowledge constitute the sphere of wisdom.

Because there is a nature of being produced, this object of knowledge follows from its associated attachments; it is through the awakening to and the thorough conceptualization of all objects of knowledge that they are therefore called "objects of knowledge" (*jñeya*).
Therefore, both "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) and "the knowledge of all-knowledge" (*sarvajñajñāna*) are like space;
they should be viewed in this way. To summarize this meaning, the verse says "all."
The term "all" (*sarva*) signifies the absence of remainder, because not even a slight portion remains.

Within this context, those among the śrāvakas who desire to realize the nirvāṇa with remainder are excluded; for although they have realized the principle of the selflessness of persons, they still grasp at the phenomena of the aggregates as being existent. Those who have realized the liberation characterized by the nirvāṇa without remainder are included here.
As the Buddha has stated, all things in every respect and in every way are empty; herein, this excludes one portion of the emptiness propounded by the non-Buddhists.
For this reason, it should be understood that within this context, there is not even the slightest phenomenon remaining in the world, and everything is like the characteristic of space.
Regarding the phrase "having the characteristic of space," one should know that this refers to the suchness of the very nature of space.

Having thus explained these nine verses, in order to further demonstrate the fruit of the various forms of knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) of the bodhisattvas and others, the following verse is stated in summary:
"By contemplating this reality according to principle, All those natures are found to have no basis."
May all the supreme aspirations for enlightenment And the adornments of great wisdom be attained.
*The Commentary on the Essential Meaning of the Nine Verses of the Noble Mother Prajñāpāramitā*, Fascicle Lower.
